name: Napu
confidence_why: One first-hand description, checked against the source; 1 other work consulted does not discuss stress.
catalog_quote: Stress is not phonemic. It occurs on the penultimate syllable of the word, except when a post-clitic is attached. [...] In Napu, statements and imperatives have falling intonation and all questions end with rising intonation which begins on the stressed syllable of the last word.

audit.action: a better source should be cited for the same classification
audit.reasoning: (1) Quote check: the deciding sentences are verbatim at Hanna & Hanna 1991 p.156 in the PDF we hold (scanned 'post-eli tic' as the record itself notes); the intonation sentence is at p.166. (2) Deciding source is a dedicated 1991 SIL phonology article by the resident fieldworkers, the only phonology in Glottolog's list; the same author's 2004 draft reference grammar (held, 230 pp) restates the rule with accent-marked minimal pairs, and the independent Indonesian Pusat Bahasa sketch (Garantjang et al. 1989, held) gives the same penultimate, predictable, non-phonemic accent. Coding fixed-strict penultimate (penultimate stress), domain word with enclitics outside the stress domain and suffixes inside, is exactly what all three say. Draft version, January 2004 (posted 'as is' without peer review). xii+216 pp. SIL International, SIL Language & Culture Archives entry 90621. [Replaces: Hanna, Roger. 2001. An introduction to the grammar of Napu: a work in progress. May 2001 draft, x+216 pp., SIL Language & Culture Archives entry 90807.] Contents: 1 Introduction; 2 Phonology (pp. 9-30); 3 Words and word class; 4 Verb classes and verbal inflection; 5 The nominal phrase; 6 The prepositional phrase; 7 The clause; 8 Clausal modifications; 9 Sentence level; 10 Discourse notes; 11 Morphology; appendices (segment positions, contrasts, three texts); references.
sources.note: Chapter 2 Phonology (pp. 9-30; 23 consonants, 5 vowels, generative-feature statement of rules) has no tone or pitch accent section, and the words 'tone', 'tonal', 'tones', 'pitch' occur nowhere in the book. The suprasegmentals treated are word stress (sec. 2.4: not phonemic, on the penultimate syllable of the word; enclitics leave stress on the root penult, true suffixes shift it to the new penult; compared with Uma), vowel length (sec. 2.5) and sentence intonation (sec. 2.9: falling in statements and imperatives, final rise from the stressed syllable of the last word in questions, extra rise…

tone.quote: This chapter describes the sound system of the Napu language. It includes sections on phonetic values (section 2.1.1), phonemes (section 2.1.2), phoneme frequency (section 2.2), syllable patterns (section 2.3), stress (section 2.4), vowel length (section 2.5), marginal phonemes (section 2.6), phonotactics (section 2.7), phonological processes (section 2.8) and sentence intonation (section 2.9). [...] Stress is not phonemic. It occurs on the penultimate syllable of the word, except when a post-clitic is attached. [...] In Napu, statements and imperatives have falling intonation and all questions end with rising intonation which begins on the stressed syllable of the last word.
